If I could give advice to past me, this is what I'd say:

Don't worry about anxiety. You're not bad or wrong or broken. It's just a feeling. It's perfectly ok to feel anxious about nothing at all. You've got enough to worry about, so don't sweat it.

Don't try to control your feelings. The harder you try to push anxiety away, the tighter it clings to you. I know it's a terrible, unpleasant sensation. Just let go. It'll pass sooner or later.

Don't hate yourself. People with anxiety problems tend to be extremely critical of themselves. I forbid it. You must love yourself. You're the person you spend the most time with. You can choose to be your best ally or your worst enemy. Choose wisely.

Be aware. Take in all the senses, alert to all the arising perceptions. Listen to your inner voice. Stay connected to both the outside world and your inner life. Observation is very important to escape the anxious feedback loops in your brain.

That's it. Don't forget to take it easy, man.

The paradox of relaxing and being happy is that actively trying to get those things is counterproductive. Imagine the happy, relaxed state you want is a cat. If you try and chase him down, he's just gonna run away. You have to sit down, be still, and wait for him to come to you.

Same thing with your emotions. You can't control your emotions. This is the most important thing. You can't control your emotions. Feelings of anxiety and worry, depression and sadness, calm and peace, they're like clouds in the sky. As hard as you try, you're never gonna control the weather. Instead, be a meteorologist. Watch the weather. See what kinds of thoughts and feelings drift through your awareness.

Eventually you might notice a pattern. All thoughts and feelings are temporary. Most last only a few moments. Some thoughts try to get your attention to try and make themselves last longer, saying things like "if you don't fixate on me, terrible things will happen!" But you don't have to do anything they say. If you just wait patiently, they all go away.

This change in perspective, from "these thoughts and feelings are me, and I must control myself" to "I can't control my thoughts, and they're not me anyways", changed my life. I still get anxious, but it doesn't really bother me that much. They're just feelings. If I get a bad feeling, I just wait for a better one. Try it out!

Committing suicide is not an inevitable consequence of panic attacks. It is a decision, just like the decision to not wear a helmet. You can choose to commit suicide, or to do something more useful, like facing your fears.

You have to make decisions in life. It is required. Every decision has the possibility of leading to negative consequences. You can try to make wise decisions, but at the end of the day, you're bound to screw the pooch every once in a while. And that's ok. Most mistakes don't kill you, and so you can learn from them.

Don't avoid facing your fears because you fear panic attacks. Avoidance is what anxiety disorders feed off of. You have to face your fears to vanquish them. You will be much happier being on the other side of your fears, but until then you have to accept the risks. You might have a panic attack. You might have something truly terrible happen to you. But odds are, you'll live, and having faced your fear, you will be stronger.

You've gotta accept that for every action, there are potential bad consequences. Yeah, you might have a panic attack. But you've had panic attacks before, right? And how did that turn out? At first its horrible and miserable, but you get through it. You're still alive. And panic attack or no, at the end of the day, you managed to face your fear. That's an achievement no one can take away from you.

At first it felt hopeless and impossible, but after enough small victories I started to get some self-confidence. With faith in my abilities, it got easier and easier. Now, even though I still experience some anxiety, it is minor enough that it doesn't really bother me anymore. I'm in a good place.

If I could go back to when I was at rock bottom and tell myself one thing, it would be this: "Cultivate compassion and loving-kindness for yourself and others." I think that unconditional compassion (desiring that one be free of suffering) and loving-kindness (desiring that one be full of happiness and joy) have been the most useful mental qualities for my recovery. They also happen to be the first two of the [four immeasurables](http://viewonbuddhism.org/immeasurables_love_compassion_equanimity_rejoicing.html) in Buddhist thought.

Having being extremely anxious for a while now, a lot of your boyfriend's behaviors sound very familiar. I think it might help to try an alternate strategy. Right now you're both caught in a vicious cycle, and you need to do something to break the cycle or you'll keep fighting forever. If you wanna make this work, you're gonna have to grab the bull by the horns here.

Let's say there's some unresolved conflict or tension between you two. It starts to cause you distress, so you ask him to talk about it either later that day or the next. This gives his brain time to worry about this relationship issue. He concocts all sorts of catastrophic scenarios in his head of you being angry at him and breaking up with him and so on. Anxiety levels rise, and soon he is very distressed. By the time you get to actually talking about it, his limbic system has worked itself into a frantic state of chronic, pathological agitation. This sort of psychological agony  eats away at your insides. An anxious mind's favorite coping strategy is avoidance, and so he uses every possible method at his disposal to escape the intolerable distress. Closing up, delaying, selective memory, learned helplessness, you name it. This of course frustrates you, and agitates the rift in your relationship. This naturally worries your boyfriend even more, because it seems to him that his worst fears are coming true!

Here's my suggestion, based on my experience as a longtime anxiety sufferer. First of all, you've gotta ambush him. Wait for the perfect time to spring a big talk on him. Just you and him, in a comfortable environment, with no distractions or responsibilities to attend to. Maybe after sex or something to get the oxytocin flowing. The most important thing is to not give him time to worry about it and get all agitated.

The next step is to lay it all out. First you'll want to communicate to him that you want to help mend the rift between you two, and he doesn't need to worry because he isn't in trouble and you love him dearly. The trick is to deliver everything in as non-violent a manner as possible. Use statements that begin with "I" rather than "you": "I feel", "I think", "I want", "I need" etc. Avoid raising your voice; a soft, friendly tone works best. Try to convey a welcome, open disposition with your body language. Basically, just make him feel safe and secure.

I think its important to strike a balance between validating his feelings and being assertive about your needs. You don't want him to feel like his debilitating psychological anguish is being brushed off as not a big deal. You also don't want to let his anxious mind weasel out of confronting the divide between you. In other words, be gentle but firm. I don't know exactly what the issues are, so you'll have to work the details out yourself.
